title: RAG as a librarian

beats.say: How can a chatbot answer questions about your company's private documents, when it has never read them?

show.sub: Yet it answers from your documents

beats.say: Think of a librarian. You ask a question. She doesn't memorize every book. She walks to the shelves, pulls three relevant pages, and reads them to you.
That is retrieval-augmented generation. Retrieval means fetching the right pages. Generation means the model writing an answer from them. And she tells you which book each page came from.

show.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
items: Generation: the model writes the answer
Citation: name the source of each page

beats.say: But the shelves must be built first. Someone collects the documents, cuts them into pages, and files them with labels. That filing work is a data pipeline, and it is most of the job.

check.q: In the librarian analogy, what does the model do with the pages that were fetched?
opts: It memorizes them permanently
It writes an answer from them and says where they came from
It rewrites the original books
check.why: The model does not store your documents. It reads the retrieved pages at question time, answers from them, and cites the source.

work: List the document sources a chatbot would need, such as runbooks, tickets and wiki pages, and who owns each.
Explain RAG to a non-technical colleague using the librarian story.

title: Ingest path and query path

beats.say: What actually happens between your question and a cited answer?

Two paths. Ingest runs in batch. It reads a runbook, cleans it, and splits it into chunks of about five hundred words. It redacts personal data, turns each chunk into a vector using an embedding model, and writes it to an index with metadata like source, version, and team.
The query path runs online. Embed the question. Filter to documents this user may see. Search for the top ten chunks closest in meaning. Optionally re-rank them down to the best four.
Then build a prompt with those four chunks, and ask the model to answer and cite them. Ingest is a pipeline. Query is a service.

show.title: Two halves, two disciplines
items: Prompt: four chunks plus a cite-your-sources rule

check.q: Why is the permission filter applied on the query path using chunk metadata?
opts: So the search runs faster on smaller vectors
So each user only gets chunks from documents they are allowed to see
So the model can choose which chunks to cite
check.why: Metadata written at ingest lets the query service restrict results per user before anything reaches the prompt.

work: Draw your own RAG system as two boxes, ingest and query, and name the owner of each.
Decide which metadata fields you must store with every chunk: source, version, owner, permissions.

title: Where RAG pipelines break

beats.say: Your wiki page was edited yesterday. Why does the bot still quote the old version?

show.sub: The wiki changed, the bot did not

beats.say: Because the index is a copy. If ingest is not incremental and idempotent, edits leave stale chunks behind, and reruns create duplicates. Fix it by keying each chunk on document id, version, and position, then deleting old chunks when a document changes.
Second trap: vectors from different embedding models are not comparable. Change the model and you must re-embed everything, a backfill, into a new index, then switch over.
Third: access control. Filter by permissions at query time, using metadata stored with each chunk, or the bot leaks secrets. Keep lineage from chunk to source, so every citation is checkable.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Lineage: chunk to document and version

check.q: You switch to a new embedding model. What must you do?
opts: Nothing, old and new vectors mix fine
Re-embed all chunks into a new index and then switch queries over
Only embed new documents from now on
check.why: Each model creates its own vector space, so distances across models are meaningless. A full backfill into a new index is required.

work: Check that your chunk ids are built from document id, version and position, so reruns do not duplicate.
Store the embedding model name on every chunk, so a migration is traceable.
Test that a user without access to a document never gets its chunks back.

title: When RAG is the wrong tool

beats.say: Should every question go through RAG?

Often no. If the answer lives in one table, run a SQL query. If the corpus is small, a few thousand words, just put it all in the prompt. RAG earns its place when the corpus is large and changes often.

show.title: Choose the simpler tool first
items: Answer in a table: use SQL
Tiny corpus: put it all in the prompt

beats.say: Costs sit mostly in ingest. Embedding ten million chunks is a one-time bill, but every model change repeats it. Index memory grows with chunk count and vector size, so plan storage and refresh cadence.
Set query budgets: latency under two seconds, cache repeated questions, log what was retrieved. Invest in quality checks on chunks and retrieval tests, because a better model can't fix bad retrieval.

check.q: A team has a 3,000 word policy document that rarely changes. What is the best design?
opts: Build a full RAG pipeline with re-ranking
Put the document directly in the prompt
Fine-tune a model on it every week
check.why: At that size the document fits in the prompt, so a pipeline, index and backfills add cost and failure modes with no benefit.

work: Write a one page decision note: SQL, full prompt, or RAG, for each of your use cases.
Estimate the re-embedding cost for your chunk count, and plan for it on every model change.
Create a small test set of questions with known source passages to measure retrieval.

title: Do you need a new database for vectors?

beats.say: Your company wants smart search. Do you really need to build a whole new building to store it?

show.sub: Or use the one you have

beats.say: Think of a library. The books you own already sit on shelves you already pay for. Adding a new section is easy. Building a second library across town is a big project.

show.title: Add a *section*, not a new library

beats.say: Vectors are just lists of numbers that capture meaning, so similar things sit close together. Your existing database can hold them beside your normal data, with the same locks and rules.
Only when the crowd gets huge, or visitors need answers instantly, do you build the second library.

show.sub: That is when you add a new system

check.q: What is the sensible first home for vectors in most teams?
opts: A dedicated vector database
The database you already run, such as Postgres
A spreadsheet
check.why: Existing systems already give you transactions and access rules. A new system is justified only by scale or latency.

work: List where your embeddable data already lives today.
Ask what extra system a vector database would force you to run and secure.

title: Exact versus approximate search

beats.say: How do you find the ten most similar vectors out of twenty million, without comparing all twenty million?

Exact search compares your query with every vector. It is perfect, but it scans everything, so it slows as data grows. An approximate index, like HNSW or IVF, jumps to a promising neighbourhood and checks only a few thousand vectors.

The price is recall. Recall at k means how many of the true top k results the index really returns. Run exact and indexed search on sample queries and compare. Ninety five percent or better may be fine.
Postgres with pgvector handles tens of millions this way, right next to your application tables.

check.q: What does recall at k measure for an approximate index?
opts: How fast the query runs
How many of the true top k results it returns
How much memory the index uses
check.why: Approximate indexes may miss true neighbours. Recall at k compares their results with exact search.

work: Take 100 real queries and compute recall at 10 with and without the index.
Tune index settings until recall meets your target, then measure latency.

title: Hybrid search and filter traps

beats.say: Why does a search for error code E four oh four seven return pages about general failures, not that exact code?

Vectors capture meaning, not spelling. Rare ids, names and codes get blurred. Keyword ranking, like BM25, matches exact tokens. Hybrid search runs both and merges the two ranked lists, often with reciprocal rank fusion.
Filters are the second trap. If you filter by team after the index returns the top ten, you may be left with two results, or none. Filter during the search, and test your most selective filters.

show.title: Filter gotchas
items: Test the rarest team and date filters

beats.say: Also, indexes need tuning as data grows, and embeddings from different models can never be mixed.

show.title: Also watch
items: Re-embed everything when the model changes

check.q: Why can filtering by team after the vector search return too few results?
opts: The index returned only the top k overall, and many belong to other teams
Filters delete vectors
Keyword search is disabled
check.why: Post-filtering throws away results from a small top k list. Filtering during the search keeps k results.

work: Build a test set with exact ids and error codes and check hybrid finds them.
Try your narrowest filter and confirm you still get k results.

title: Choosing where vectors live

beats.say: When is pgvector the wrong choice, and what would you pick instead?

Start where the data lives. Postgres gives transactions, access rules and one system to run. The warehouse suits batch jobs and analytics, because data never leaves, but its latency is too high for user-facing search.

Move to a dedicated vector database at hundreds of millions of vectors, with tight latency at high query rates and heavy filtering. You pay with a second system to sync, secure and monitor, and copies that can drift.

show.title: Cost of a new system
items: Another system to monitor and pay for

beats.say: My rule: pgvector or the warehouse first, hybrid search with metadata filters, and migrate only when measured recall or latency fails.

check.q: What justifies moving to a dedicated vector database?
opts: It is newer technology
Measured scale, latency or filtering needs your current system cannot meet
The team wants to try it
check.why: A second system adds sync, security and ops cost, so only evidence that the current one fails justifies it.

work: Write down your latency, recall and scale targets before choosing a store.
Load test pgvector at projected vector counts and query rates.
Keep embeddings reproducible so migrating stores stays cheap.

title: The catalog that lies

beats.say: What happens when a library catalog still lists a book that was thrown away?

A search index for an AI assistant is that catalog. It points to small pieces of your documents. If a policy is rewritten or deleted, but the catalog keeps the old page, the assistant quotes it with total confidence.

The fix starts with a fingerprint, called a hash. It is a short code that changes whenever the text changes. Compare today's fingerprints with yesterday's. Only redo pages that changed, and remove entries for pages that vanished.
Rebuilding everything every night works, but it is like re-cataloging the whole library for one new book. It wastes money.

show.text: One new book, not the whole library

check.q: What is a hash used for here?
opts: To make search faster
To spot which documents changed
To compress the documents
check.why: A hash is a fingerprint of the text. If it differs from last time, the document changed and needs redoing; if it matches, skip it.

work: List which of your document sources can be rewritten or deleted without telling anyone.
Ask how often your index is rebuilt and what that costs per run.

title: Embed only what changed

beats.say: You have 100,000 documents. Only 200 changed today. Why re-embed all of them?

Step one: hash each document's text and store the hash beside its chunks. Step two: on each run, hash again and compare. An unseen document is new. A different hash means changed. A missing document means deleted.
Embed only the 200. Replace their old chunks, and delete chunks of removed documents. That is about 200 embedding calls instead of 100,000, a cut of 99.8 percent in cost.
Key each chunk by document id, chunk number, and content hash. Then a retry overwrites instead of duplicating.

show.title: Idempotent upsert key
show.text:
key = doc_id + chunk_no + content_hash
upsert(key, vector)  # retry-safe

check.q: Why key chunks by doc id, chunk number and content hash?
opts: So a retried write replaces rather than duplicates
So chunks sort alphabetically
So embeddings are smaller
check.why: A deterministic key means writing the same chunk twice hits the same record, making retries safe (idempotent).

work: Store a content hash per document next to its chunks.
Log how many documents were new, changed and deleted on every run.

title: Orphans, deletes and model changes

beats.say: Your document shrank from ten chunks to eight. Where did chunks nine and ten go?
Nowhere. They stay in the index as orphans, still answering questions with old text. So an update must delete every chunk of that document that is not in the new set, not just upsert the new ones.

Deletes are the dangerous case. A hash scan only notices a missing document if you list the source fully. Change data capture, which streams inserts, updates and deletes from the database log, catches them immediately. This matters for right to be forgotten requests, which cover vectors too.
One more trap: changing the embedding model makes old vectors incomparable, so that needs a full rebuild. Track the model version too.

check.q: A document shrinks from 10 chunks to 8. What must the update do?
opts: Upsert the 8 new chunks only
Upsert the 8 and delete the document's other chunks
Re-embed the whole corpus
check.why: Upserts never remove chunks 9 and 10, so they linger as orphans. Delete chunks of that document absent from the new set.

work: Write a test: shrink a document and assert its extra chunks disappear.
Record the embedding model version on every chunk.
Document how a delete request reaches the vector index.

title: Scan or stream: choosing freshness

beats.say: Should you stream every change, or just scan nightly? It depends on how costly a stale answer is.

show.sub: Price the cost of a stale answer

beats.say: A nightly hash scan is simple and works on any source, including file shares. But lag is up to a day, and deletes can slip. CDC gives seconds of lag but needs log access, ordering, and a consumer you must operate.

Use CDC for policies, pricing, and anything legal. Use scans for wikis and manuals. Whatever you pick, export two metrics: lag between source change and index, and count of orphan chunks whose source is gone. Alert when either drifts.
For a model change, build a second index alongside, then switch traffic over. Never re-embed in place.

check.q: Which source most justifies the cost of CDC?
opts: A team wiki updated weekly
Legal policies where stale or undeleted content is risky
Archived manuals
check.why: CDC adds operational cost, so spend it where stale answers or missed deletes carry legal or financial risk.

work: Tier your sources by staleness risk and assign scan or CDC to each tier.
Dashboard index lag and orphan chunk count with alert thresholds.
Plan a blue-green index swap for the next embedding model upgrade.

title: Grading the helper and the writer

beats.say: Your study buddy gave a wrong answer. Was the buddy careless, or did they grab the wrong book?
RAG is an open-book exam. A helper fetches pages from a huge library. Then a writer answers using only those pages.
So grade two things. Did the helper bring back the pages that hold the answer? And did the writer stick to those pages, without inventing anything?
Grade them separately. If the helper fetched the wrong pages, even a brilliant writer fails, and polishing the writer wastes your time.

check.q: A RAG system gives wrong answers because the helper keeps fetching the wrong pages. What should you do first?
opts: Rewrite the writer's instructions
Fix how the helper finds pages
Use a bigger writer model
check.why: A writer can only use what it receives. When the wrong pages arrive, improving the writer cannot help. Grading the two halves separately shows where the fault is.

work: Write down which half you would blame for each wrong answer: fetching or writing.
Collect ten real questions and note which document should answer each.

title: Recall at k and faithfulness

beats.say: How do you turn 'the search seems okay' into a number?
Build a labelled set. Say two hundred questions, each tagged with the chunks that truly answer it.
Run each question and look at the top five results. If two chunks answer it and one appears, recall at five is one half. Then average across all two hundred.

Next, grade the answer. Is every claim supported by the retrieved chunks? Code can check that cited ids really exist. A judge model with a rubric scores the rest, once you compare it with human labels.

show.title: Grading generation
items: Rubric judge, calibrated on human labels

check.q: A question has 4 answer chunks and the top 5 results contain 3 of them. What is recall at 5?
check.why: Recall at k is found answer chunks divided by all labelled answer chunks. Three of four is 0.75.

work: Label 50 real questions with the chunks that answer them.
Compute recall at 5 and recall at 10 and keep the numbers as a baseline.

title: Where the metrics mislead

beats.say: Recall is ninety percent, yet users still complain. How?
Recall at k only says the right chunk was somewhere in the top k. It ignores rank. If it sits at position nine and the model only reads three, the answer still fails.
Faithfulness has its own trap. A citation can point to a real chunk that does not support the claim. An id check passes, but the answer is still wrong.

Judges drift and favor long answers, so recheck them against human labels. Labelled sets go stale as documents change. Rerun the eval on every change to chunking, embeddings, index settings or prompt.

show.title: Keep the eval honest
items: Recheck the judge against human labels

check.q: Every cited chunk id in an answer exists in the index. What does that prove?
opts: The answer is faithful
The citations are well formed, nothing more
The retrieval recall is high
check.why: An id check only shows the citation points at something real. Whether that chunk supports the claim needs a faithfulness check.

work: Report recall at several k values, not only one.
Sample 30 judged answers each month and compare them to human grades.

title: Running an eval you can afford

beats.say: Your eval passes, but the bill doubles. Did you measure the right things?

show.sub: Quality is only part of the picture

beats.say: Retrieval and generation quality are only half the picture. Track latency per stage, cost per answer, cache hit rate, and index lag, meaning how stale the newest documents are.
Labels are expensive, so start with fifty real questions from logs and grow. Use cheap code checks on every run, and the costly judge on a sample or on changes.

chip.text: Cheap first, costly on a sample

beats.say: Gate releases on it. If recall drops, block the change and fix chunking, filters or hybrid search first. Don't tune prompts to hide a retrieval problem.

check.q: A change to chunking lowers recall at 5 from 0.82 to 0.70, but the answers look fine in a quick test. What do you do?
opts: Ship it, since the answers look fine
Block it and investigate retrieval
Edit the prompt to compensate
check.why: A recall drop is a measured regression that a quick test can miss. Gate on it and fix retrieval, rather than hiding the problem in the prompt.

work: Add the labelled eval to CI so every chunking, embedding, index or prompt change runs it.
Log per-stage latency, cost per answer and index lag on a dashboard next to quality.

title: The mailroom clerk with a form

beats.say: How do you get a fare and a city out of a messy complaint email?
Picture a mailroom clerk. Every letter is different. The clerk copies the city, the fare and the date onto a printed form. That form is the schema: fixed boxes, fixed kinds of answer.
Clerks make mistakes. So a checker looks at each form. A date in the fare box? Hand it back once with a note. Still wrong? It goes in a tray for a manager to read.
A language model is that clerk. Fast, but sometimes it guesses. So you never trust the form until it is checked.

show.text: Never trust the form until it is checked
show.sub: The model is a fast, sometimes guessing clerk

check.q: In the clerk story, what does the checker stand for?
opts: Code that validates every extracted row
A bigger model that rewrites the email
A backup copy of the original letters
check.why: The checker is plain code that tests each row against the schema, so a guessing model cannot silently put bad data into your tables.

work: Pick one free-text source, like support emails, and write down the three fields you would want as columns.
Define each field's type and allowed values before you write any prompt.

title: Extraction with a contract

beats.say: What happens when a model reads ten thousand complaint emails and one answer comes back as banana?

show.sub: One bad row in ten thousand still breaks a report

beats.say: First, define a schema. Fare must be a number above zero. Date must be a real date. Status must be one of three allowed words. Your code checks every row against it, not the model.

show.title: The schema, checked in code
items: status: one of three allowed words
Checked by your code, not by the model

beats.say: If a row fails, retry once, and send the error message back to the model. Fare is not a number, try again. If it fails twice, write it to a dead-letter table, a holding pen, for a person to review.
Add model, prompt version and extracted at to each row. When the prompt changes, you can re-run only the old rows. And label two hundred emails by hand to measure accuracy per field.

show.title: Make it re-runnable and measurable
items: Backfill only rows from old versions

check.q: A row fails validation twice. What should happen?
opts: Retry until it passes
Write it to a dead-letter table for human review
Drop it silently so the load finishes
check.why: Retries are bounded so cost and time stay predictable. Rows that still fail go to a dead-letter table where a person can inspect them, instead of being lost or retried forever.

work: Add model, prompt_version and extracted_at columns to any LLM-filled table.
Create a dead-letter table and alert when its row count grows past a threshold.

title: Valid but wrong

beats.say: Your extracted row passed validation. So why can the fare still be wrong?

show.text: Valid is not the same as true

beats.say: A schema checks shape, not truth. A fare of forty dollars is a valid number even if the email said fourteen. The model may also guess a missing field instead of leaving it empty. Allow null, and tell it to use it.
Overall accuracy hides weak spots. Date might be ninety-nine percent right while fare is eighty-five. Measure each field against your hand-labelled sample.
Also, the email is untrusted input. Text saying ignore your instructions can hijack the model. Treat output as data, validate it, never run it. Long emails can get truncated, so check lengths.

show.title: More failure modes
items: Prompt injection hidden in the document

check.q: Which problem can a schema check NOT catch?
opts: Fare returned as text instead of a number
A valid-looking fare that does not match the email
Status outside the allowed list
check.why: Types, formats and allowed values are shape checks. A plausible but incorrect value passes them, which is why you also need a labelled sample to measure real accuracy.

work: Build a labelled sample of about 200 documents and report accuracy per field, not one overall number.
Allow null for every optional field and count how often it is used.

title: Privacy: every copy is a leak

beats.say: You deleted a customer's email from the database. Is their phone number gone?

show.text: Deleted from the table. Gone everywhere?

beats.say: Not necessarily. Prompts, logs, caches and vector indexes are all new copies of your data. Each one can leak.
So redact first. Replace emails, phone numbers and names with placeholders at ingestion, before text reaches any model or index. Once a number is embedded, it is hard to pull back out.
Then add an access label to every chunk, like team or clearance. At query time, filter by who is asking, so a person retrieves only what they may read. Filter before ranking, not after.

show.title: Access control at query time
items: Label every chunk with who may read it
Filter by the asker's access in the query
Same question, different people, different answers

check.q: When is the right moment to redact personal data?
opts: After the answer is shown to the user
At ingestion, before text reaches a model or an index
Only when a deletion request arrives
check.why: Once personal data is in a prompt log, cache or embedding, you have copies to chase. Redacting at ingestion stops those copies from ever holding it.

work: List every place text is copied in your RAG pipeline: prompts, logs, caches, indexes.
Add an access label to each chunk and test that a low-privilege user retrieves nothing restricted.

title: Do you need a model here?

beats.say: Should every document go through a large language model?

Often no. If the format is fixed, like invoices from one supplier, a regex or parser is free, instant and repeatable. A model call can cost a fraction of a cent, but across fifty million documents that is real money, plus seconds of latency.
Use a cheap model first, escalate hard cases to a bigger one, and batch overnight when nobody waits. Cache by document hash so you never pay twice.
For sensitive text, weigh a self-hosted model against redaction plus a vendor under contract. Choose by risk: if a wrong field costs money or law, keep a human in the loop.

show.title: Choose by risk
items: Self-hosted: control, but you run it
Vendor: redact first, contract the rest

check.q: Invoices from one supplier always have the same layout. What is the best first choice?
opts: A large model for every invoice
A rule-based parser, with a model only for exceptions
Manual typing by staff
check.why: A fixed layout is cheap, fast and deterministic to parse with rules. Keep the model for the odd cases where the layout varies, which controls cost and variance.

work: Estimate cost per million documents for rules, a small model and a large model, then pick the cheapest that meets your accuracy target.
Add a document-hash cache so unchanged files are never re-extracted.

title: A map where meaning has a place

beats.say: How can a computer find the right paragraph when your question uses none of the same words as the page?

Picture a huge city map. Every paragraph of text gets a pin. Paragraphs about the same idea land close together, even with different words. Those pins are called embeddings. An embedding is just a list of numbers, like map coordinates, that says where a meaning sits.
You cannot pin a whole book as one spot, because it talks about too many things. So you cut it into pieces called chunks, like index cards. One idea per card.
When you ask a question, it gets a pin too. We simply hand back the cards whose pins sit nearest to it.

check.q: In the map analogy, what does an embedding represent?
opts: The full text of a paragraph stored compressed
Coordinates that place a paragraph's meaning so similar ideas sit close
A keyword list used for exact matching
check.why: An embedding is a list of numbers acting as coordinates for meaning, so similar ideas land near each other even with different words.

work: Take one real question your users ask and find a page that answers it using different words.
Explain to a non-technical teammate why a book is cut into chunks before it is pinned.

title: Embeddings and cosine similarity

beats.say: How does a machine decide that two sentences mean the same thing?
An embedding model turns text into a vector, say seven hundred sixty eight numbers. Each text becomes an arrow in space. Similar meanings point in nearly the same direction.
To compare, we measure the angle between two arrows. That is cosine similarity. After normalising, so every arrow has length one, a score near one means the same meaning. Near zero means unrelated.
At query time, embed the question with the same model, then fetch the top five closest chunks. Mix models, and the numbers live in different spaces, so the scores mean nothing.

check.q: A cosine similarity near one between a query and a chunk means what?
opts: The two vectors point in nearly the same direction, so meanings are close
The chunk contains the exact words of the query
The chunk is nearly one word long
check.why: Cosine measures the angle between normalised vectors. A small angle, score near one, means similar meaning, not matching words.

work: Check that the query path and the indexing path call the exact same embedding model and version.
Print the top five scores for a few real questions to see what a good match and a bad match look like.

title: Chunk size decides what can be found

beats.say: Why does chunk size decide whether the right answer is ever found?

show.sub: Too big or too small both fail

beats.say: Too big, say three thousand words, and one chunk mixes five topics. Its vector is blurry, and your prompt fills with noise.
Too small, say twenty words, and an answer that spans two sentences gets cut at the boundary. Neither half is retrieved whole.

A sensible start is two hundred to four hundred words, with ten to twenty percent overlap. A three hundred word chunk then repeats about forty five words from its neighbour. Split on headings and paragraphs first. Keep the heading path, like Runbook, Kafka, Consumer lag, with the chunk.

show.title: A sensible starting point
items: Split on headings and paragraphs first
Keep the heading path in metadata and often in the text

check.q: Which problem is most likely if chunks are 20 words each?
opts: Each vector mixes many topics and becomes blurry
An answer spanning sentences is split and never retrieved whole
The embedding model refuses short text
check.why: Tiny chunks cut answers at boundaries, so neither piece holds the full answer. Blurry vectors are the problem of oversized chunks.

work: Chunk a sample of 20 real documents at 300 words with 15 percent overlap and read ten chunks by eye.
Add the heading path to each chunk's text and metadata, then compare retrieval on five known questions.

title: Lineage: what to store with every vector

beats.say: A year from now, someone asks which document produced a wrong answer. Can you tell?

show.sub: A vector alone can't tell you

beats.say: Only if each chunk stores its document id, chunk number, text, content hash, embedding model name, embedded time, and access labels.

show.title: One chunk record
show.text:
doc_id
chunk_no
text
content_hash
embedding_model
embedded_at
access_labels

beats.say: The content hash lets you skip re-embedding unchanged chunks, which saves cost when a document is edited. The access labels let you filter out chunks a user may not see, before the prompt is built.
The model name matters most. Vectors from two models cannot be compared. Without the name, you cannot even tell which vectors are stale.

chip.text: Store the model name per vector

check.q: Why store the embedding model name with every vector?
opts: It makes cosine similarity faster
Vectors from different models are not comparable, so you must know which are which
It is needed to compress the vectors
check.why: Different models produce different spaces. Recording the model lets you detect mixed or stale vectors and plan a re-embed.

work: Audit your chunk table for doc_id, chunk_no, content_hash, embedding_model, embedded_at and access labels.
Add a nightly job that re-embeds only chunks whose content hash changed.

title: Changing the embedding model safely

beats.say: A vendor releases a better embedding model. Do you just switch?
No. A new model is a new space, so old vectors are useless beside it. You re-embed every chunk into a brand new index, while the old one keeps serving users.

show.title: Build the new index *beside* the old

beats.say: Cost scales with chunks. Ten million chunks of 400 words is several billion tokens to embed, plus index build time and double storage during the move.
Before the switch, run both indexes against your eval set of real questions with known right chunks. Compare hit rate. Cut over only if the new one wins, and keep the old one for rollback.

check.q: What is the safest way to adopt a new embedding model?
opts: Re-embed only new documents with the new model
Overwrite vectors in place, one chunk at a time
Re-embed everything into a new index, compare on an eval set, then switch
check.why: Mixed models in one index give meaningless scores. A parallel index lets you measure quality first and roll back cheaply.

work: Build an eval set of 50 real questions with the right chunk labelled for each.
Estimate re-embed cost now: chunk count times average tokens times price, plus double storage.

title: Search is a pipeline, not one lookup

beats.say: Why does the demo find the right page, but the real assistant over ten million documents does not?
In production, every question runs a short pipeline. First rewrite it into a clear search query. Then search by keywords and by meaning at the same time.
Then a slower, smarter model rereads the best fifty and keeps the top five. And every step only sees what this user is allowed to read.

show.title: Then
items: Only what this user may read

beats.say: Each step is cheap enough to fit inside a two-second answer.

check.q: What does the reranking step do?
opts: Rereads the best few dozen and keeps the top handful
Searches the whole index again with a larger model
Rewrites the question into several new questions
check.why: A reranker scores only the fused candidates, question and passage together, and keeps the best few for the prompt.

beats.say: Keyword search and vector search each return a ranked list. How do you merge them?
Their scores are on different scales, so averaging them lets one side win by accident. Reciprocal rank fusion uses only positions: each list adds one over sixty plus the rank.
A document ranked first by keywords and third by vectors beats one that only one search liked.
Keywords catch error codes and ticket numbers. Vectors catch meaning. Fusion keeps both.

check.q: Why not simply average BM25 and cosine scores?
opts: They sit on different scales, so one side dominates
Averages take too long to compute for each query
Cosine scores are always larger than BM25 scores
check.why: BM25 is unbounded and cosine sits between -1 and 1; RRF sidesteps that by using ranks.

beats.say: An engineer asks the assistant about salaries, and it quotes a document only HR may open. Where did it go wrong?
Every chunk carries its document's groups as labels. The query passes the user's groups into the search as a filter, so a forbidden chunk is never ranked, reranked or sent to the model.
Keep labels fresh with the same change capture as the content, and key every cache by permission set.
A prompt that says do not reveal is not access control.

show.text: The prompt is not a lock

check.q: Why is filtering after ranking risky?
opts: Results can run short, and anything shown has leaked
It makes the vector index much larger on disk
It stops keyword search from finding any matches
check.why: Post-filtering can starve the top results, and anything a model or user already saw cannot be taken back.

title: A latency budget for every stage

beats.say: An interviewer asks: your answer must start within two seconds. Where does the time go?
Rewriting takes a hundred milliseconds or so, and you skip it for short keyword queries. Embedding the question and both searches, run in parallel, take well under a hundred.
Reranking fifty passages costs about a hundred. Everything left goes to the model, starting to stream the answer.
Name each stage, give it a number, and measure it separately. That is the answer they want.

show.text: Name it, number it, measure it

check.q: Which part of a RAG answer usually takes most of a two-second budget?
opts: Reranking the fifty fused candidates
The model generating the answer
Embedding the user's question
check.why: Retrieval and reranking fit in a few hundred milliseconds; the model producing tokens takes the rest.

beats.say: Two runbooks give different timeouts. Which one does the assistant believe?
Retrieval cannot tell on its own. So store the date, the version and how authoritative the source is with every chunk: a policy beats a wiki page, and a wiki page beats a chat message.
Then prefer the newest authoritative chunk, and have the assistant say that another source disagrees, citing both.
And tell the document owners: a stale page still in the index is a freshness bug.

check.q: Two indexed sources disagree. What should the assistant do?
opts: Pick one at random and answer confidently
Prefer the newest authoritative one and say they disagree
Refuse to answer any question on that topic
check.why: Dates and authority decide; showing the conflict with both citations keeps the reader in control.

title: Citations you can check, and saying I don't know

beats.say: How do you know an answer did not make something up?
Ask for every claim with the ids of the chunks it came from. Then check in code that each id was in the prompt, and that any quote really appears in that chunk.
And when the best match scores below a threshold you tuned on labelled questions, do not call the model at all. Say nothing reliable was found, and show the closest documents.
A system that never says I don't know is guessing.

check.q: What should happen when no retrieved passage scores above your tuned threshold?
opts: Answer from the model's own memory instead
Say nothing reliable was found and show the closest
Lower the threshold until something passes it
check.why: Abstaining below a tuned score avoids confident made-up answers, and you measure correct refusals on unanswerable questions.

beats.say: Models now read a million tokens. Why not put every document in the prompt and skip retrieval?
For a few contracts or one manual that rarely changes, do exactly that, with prompt caching. It is the simplest system there is.
But every query pays for every token, facts in the middle of a huge prompt get missed, and you cannot hide documents some users may not see.

show.title: RAG wins
items: Cost and latency at high query rates

beats.say: The middle way: retrieve the best few documents, then give the model those documents whole.

check.q: When is long context a better choice than RAG?
opts: A small corpus that rarely changes
Ten million documents changing daily
Users who may see different documents
check.why: Long context suits small, stable corpora; large, changing or permissioned corpora still need retrieval.

title: GraphRAG, and when it is worth it

beats.say: What are the main complaint themes across fifty thousand tickets? Vector search cannot answer that: the answer is spread everywhere.

GraphRAG has a model pull people, products and relations out of every document into a graph, groups it into communities, and summarises each group. Global questions read the summaries; multi-hop ones walk the graph.
The price: a model call over the whole corpus to build it, its own extraction errors, and hard refreshes.
If the relations already live in tables, a SQL join is cheaper and exact.

check.q: When is GraphRAG worth its indexing cost?
opts: Simple lookups of one passage
Global themes and multi-hop questions
Any corpus that changes every hour
check.why: GraphRAG helps with questions whose answer spans many documents; its build cost and refresh difficulty make it a poor default.

title: RAG: answers from your own documents

beats.say: How does an assistant answer from this morning's runbook, when the model was trained a year ago?
Retrieval-augmented generation finds the few passages that matter, puts them in the prompt, and asks the model to answer only from them, with citations.
Fine-tuning teaches style and format, not new facts, and it cannot forget a deleted document or respect who may see what.
That is why most company assistants you meet at work are built on retrieval.

check.q: Why do company assistants usually use RAG rather than fine-tuning for facts?
opts: Fine-tuning cannot follow changes, deletes and permissions
Fine-tuned models cannot answer questions at all
RAG needs no data pipeline or index to run
check.why: Retrieval reads current documents per user; fine-tuning bakes facts in and cannot unlearn or filter them.

beats.say: Do you need a vector database on day one?
For millions of chunks, Postgres with pgvector, or your warehouse's vector functions, keeps the vectors next to the data, its backups and its access rules.
A dedicated vector database earns its place at hundreds of millions of vectors, very high query rates, or heavy filtering at that scale.
Move when your own measurements show the need for it, not before, because every new system is one more thing to run.

check.q: A team already runs Postgres and has five million chunks. Where should vectors live first?
opts: A new dedicated vector database cluster
Postgres with pgvector, next to the data
Inside every prompt, as plain text
check.why: pgvector handles this scale with the access rules and backups the team already has.

title: HNSW: how vector search is fast

beats.say: How do you find the nearest of fifty million vectors without comparing all of them?
HNSW links each vector to its nearest neighbours in a graph with a few sparse layers on top. A search enters at the top and walks greedily towards the question, layer by layer.
More links per vector and more candidates per query mean better recall, more memory and slower queries.
Heavy filters can starve the walk, so measure recall at k with the filter on.

check.q: What does raising ef_search in an HNSW index trade?
opts: Better recall for slower queries
Less memory for worse recall
Faster builds for fewer vectors
check.why: ef_search is how many candidates a query keeps; more candidates find more true neighbours but take longer.

beats.say: Why does a second model reorder the results after the vector search?
The embedding model turns the question and each chunk into vectors separately, so chunks are embedded once, ahead of time. Fast, but it never reads them together.
A cross-encoder reads the question and one passage in a single pass and scores whether the passage answers it. Far more accurate, and one model pass per candidate.
So the first finds fifty in milliseconds, and the second picks the best five in about a hundred.

check.q: Why run the cross-encoder only on the top fifty candidates?
opts: It costs one model pass per candidate per query
It cannot read passages longer than fifty words
It only works on results from keyword search
check.why: Cross-encoders cannot be precomputed, so you run them on a small candidate set from the fast first stage.

beats.say: Ten million documents, a thousand questions a second. How much memory does the index need?
About five chunks each makes fifty million vectors. At 1,024 dimensions in 32-bit floats, that is around 205 gigabytes before the graph.
Quantize to shrink it, shard for memory, and add replicas for the query rate, with headroom for a lost zone.
The biggest cost is model tokens, eighty-six million answers a day, so keep prompts small.

check.q: What usually dominates the cost of a RAG service at 1,000 queries a second?
opts: Model tokens for every answer
Storing the vector index on disk
Embedding each user's question
check.why: Retrieval is cheap per query; generating an answer with several retrieved chunks costs the most, so prompt size is the main lever.

beats.say: RAG rarely crashes. It fails quietly, with confident answers. What goes wrong?
A deleted document is still answered from. A permission change has not reached the index. A new embedding model is mixed with old vectors.
An index setting change drops recall, and nobody notices. Or nothing relevant was found, and the model answers anyway.

show.title: Quality failures
items: No eval set to catch it

beats.say: Defences: index lag alerts, a re-embed into a new index, and an eval set rerun on every change.

check.q: Your team switches embedding models. What is the safe way to do it?
opts: Re-embed into a new index and compare on the eval set
Embed new documents with it and keep the old vectors
Switch the query side first and re-embed later on
check.why: Vectors from two models are not comparable; build a new index, compare recall, then switch.

beats.say: The assistant gives a confidently wrong answer to an on-call engineer at night. Whose problem is it, and who gets paged?
The data platform team owns the ingest pipeline: chunking, embeddings, freshness, deletes and permission labels, like any derived table.
The product team owns prompts, the eval set and answer quality. Security owns the permission model.
Split the debugging the same way. First check whether the right passage was retrieved at all; if it was, look at the prompt and the model. Retrieval first, then generation.

check.q: Who should own freshness, deletes and permission labels in the index?
opts: The product team that writes the prompts
The data platform team, as a derived table
Each user, by reporting stale answers
check.why: The index is a derived table built by a pipeline, so the platform team owns its freshness and labels.

title: When not to use RAG, and when to move off

beats.say: An architect is asked: when is RAG the wrong choice?
When the corpus fits in the context window and rarely changes. When the answer is a number in a table: use SQL. When the question spans everything: themes, multi-hop.
And when nobody will build an eval set, because then nobody will know whether it works.
Move off when long context becomes cheap for your corpus, when most questions turn out structured, or when a managed search service does the job for less.

check.q: Most questions to your assistant are about totals and counts. What should you do?
opts: Answer them with SQL or a semantic layer
Add more chunks to each prompt for them
Fine-tune the model on the tables
check.why: Numbers in tables are answered exactly by SQL; text retrieval is the wrong tool for them.
